The *New Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in seven fascicles was translated at the Great Monastery in Chang’an during the summer of the eighth year of Hongshi. The *New Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* in seven fascicles [was also then produced].
The *Huashou-jing* (Flower-Head Sūtra) in ten fascicles—also known as the *Shezhushangen-jing* (Sūtra on Gathering All Roots of Goodness)—is currently missing.
The *New Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in three fascicles was produced at the Great Monastery in Chang’an during the eighth year of Hongshi. The *New Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* [was also then produced].
The *Sūtra* in two fascicles; the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* in five fascicles (or four), which is fixed at five; translated by Kumārajīva together with Buddhayaśas;
the *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra* in four fascicles (also called the *Brahmaviśeṣacinti-paripṛcchā-sūtra*); the *Lokadhātu-sūtra* in four fascicles (or three);
the *Vajraśekhara-rāja-sūtra* in two fascicles, produced in the ninth year of Hongshi; and the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* in three fascicles.
Volume One: *The Sūtra on the Selection of All Dharmas* (also in two volumes); Volume Three:
*The Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra* (also known as the *Pūrṇa-paripṛcchā*, or alternatively in two volumes as the *Sūtra Praising the Merits of All Buddhas*); Volume Three:
*The Sūtra of the Collection of Flowers of Immeasurable Life* (one volume; also called the *Amitābha Sūtra*); *Maitreya’s Descent*.
*Śraddhā-pratilambha-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Maitreya-buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, one fascicle;
*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, one fascicle (also called *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*); *Sarvadharmāpravṛtti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, one fascicle;
*Bodhicitta-sūtra*, one fascicle (also called *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*); *Śāsanāntima-sūtra*, one fascicle (also called *The Buddha on the Verge of Parinirvāṇa*).
The *Nirvāṇa-saṃkṣipta-śikṣāpada-sūtra*, one fascicle; the *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-vipaśyanā-sūtra*, one fascicle; the *Bodhisattva-kutsita-rāga-kāma-sūtra*, one fascicle [missing];
the *Dhyāna-dharma-arthaviniścaya*, two fascicles—also called the *Dhyāna-ya-sūtra* or the *Dhyāna-sūtra*;

the *Bodhisattva-dhyāna-dharma-sūtra*, three fascicles—also known as the *Zuochan-sanmei-jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation); the *Mārga-vicitra-upamā-sūtra*, one fascicle; and the *Bhikṣu-*.
Dao-lüe translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* in one hundred fascicles at the Xiaoyao Garden; it was later divided into seventy fascicles.

He also translated the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* in sixteen fascicles, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in ten fascicles, the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* in four fascicles, the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra* in one fascicle, and the *Śata-śāstra* in two fascicles during the sixth year of Hongshi. Furthermore, he had already translated the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* in sixty-one fascicles.
*Record of Entering the Vinaya: The Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa Sūtra of the Ten Recitations*, one fascicle; *Essentials of Dhyāna Methods*, three fascicles.
Re-edited on the fifth day of the second month in the ninth year of Hongshi. The above comprises thirty-five works.
In total, there are two hundred and ninety-four fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the Indian śramaṇa Kumārajīva...
In the third year of the Hongshi era of Yao Xing of the pseudo-Qin dynasty, he arrived in Chang’an and translated [these texts] at the Great Monastery and in the Xiaoyao Garden.

The *Dīrgha Āgama* in twenty-two fascicles was produced in the fifteenth year of the Hongshi era by Zhu Fonian as the oral translator and Tanwude as the scribe. The *Mahīśāsaka Vinaya* in forty-five fascicles had already been entered into the Vinaya catalog. The *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* in one fascicle—also known as the *Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva Sūtra*—was obtained by the Tripiṭaka Master after his return to foreign lands in Jibin; it was sent to Liangzhou via merchants. The *Mahīśāsaka Prātimokṣa* in one fascicle. These constitute four works in total.
It consists of sixty-nine fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty,
the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas from Kaśmīra [translated it].
Translated at Chang’an during the Hongshi era of Yao Xing;
one work in twenty-two (or twenty) fascicles: the *Śāriputrābhidharma*.
It consists of twenty-two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty,
there was a foreign śramaṇa named Vighna.
Translated at Shiyang Monastery in Chang’an for Yao Xing.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in thirty-six fascicles was translated on the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the tenth year of the Xuanshi era by Juqu Mengxun, the illegitimate King of Hexi.
The *Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* in twenty-nine fascicles was also translated [by him]; some say—
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, in either thirty fascicles or twenty-four fascicles; the *Vaipulyarāja-gaganagañja-sūtra* in five fascicles, also called the *Mahāgaganagañja-sūtra*.
Upon examining the scriptural text, it is identical to the "Gaganagañja-parivarta," the eighth chapter of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*;
it is unclear whether this is a separate excerpt or not. It is not recorded separately. [Compiled by] the Śramaṇa Qifu during the Qi dynasty in the kingdom of Henan.
Translated by Shi Shengjian: the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāmegha Sūtra* in four fascicles (also known as the *Vaipulya Amala-mahāmegha Sūtra*), or in six fascicles;
the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in ten fascicles (according to the *Lidai Sanbao Ji*); the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* in four fascicles, said to have been brought out by Gong Shang;
the *Sāgaranāgarāja-paripṛcchā Sūtra* in four fascicles; and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* in eight fascicles (also known as the *Bodhisattva*).
The *Śīlasūtra* (or alternatively the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*), the *Bodhisattva-śīla-mūla* in one fascicle; separately listed:
the *Upāsaka-śīla* in seven fascicles from Dunhuang, the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* in eight fascicles, and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-upāsaka-śīla-maṇḍala-vinaya* in one fascicle.
The above comprises eleven works.
In all, it consists of one hundred and four fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty,
the Indian śramaṇa Dharmakṣema [translated this].
He arrived at Xiliangzhou and, for the ruler of the pseudo-Hexi state, Da Zuqu Mengxun, translated what is also known as *Dharmakṣema*’s *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* in sixty fascicles.
It was begun in the fourth month of the Dingchou year and completed in the seventh month of the Jimao year. This constitutes one work.
It consists of sixty fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty,
the śramaṇa from Liangzhou, Shi Daotai, collaborated with the śramaṇa from the Western Regions, Buddhabhadra.
It was translated within the Yuanyu Palace Temple in the city of Liangzhou.
Initially, one hundred fascicles were produced,
but shortly thereafter, the state fell into chaos and perished due to the rebellion of the great King Juqu of Liang.
Forty fascicles of the sūtra text were lost;
the remaining sixty fascicles were transmitted to the capital.
*Ratnarāśi-sūtra*, two fascicles: this constitutes one work.
It consists of two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Shi Daogong translated it at Liangzhou. It is said to have been produced there.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, fifty fascicles: the śramaṇa Zhīfǎlǐng obtained the Hu-language manuscript of this sūtra in the kingdom of Yutian.
Upon arriving in the Jin dynasty, on the tenth day of the third month in the fourteenth year of the Yìxī era, he began the translation at Dào-chǎng Temple;
it was completed on the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Yǒngchū era of the Song dynasty. [This concludes] the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.
The *Sūtra* in eight fascicles; the new *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* in two fascicles; translated at the Daochang Monastery in the second year of the Yongchu era, the *Dhyāna-sūtra:

Methods for Practice* in two fascicles—also titled *Gaṅgācarabhūmi*, which translates as *The Ground of Practice*, or *The Sūtra on the Meditation on Impurity*—containing seventeen chapters in total; and the *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* in one fascicle.
Some say that the following texts of the Tathāgatagarbha [tradition] are currently missing:

one fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra*, one fascicle of the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle of the *Abhinava-guhyaka-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, one fascicle of the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* (missing), one fascicle of the *Viśuddha-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* (missing), and one fascicle of the *Mañjuśrī-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (missing). [These were recorded during] the second year of the Yuánxī era of the Jìn dynasty.
In the year Gengshen, at Daochang Temple, the aforementioned ten sections were produced,
totaling sixty-seven fascicles,
during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty.
The Indian Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra arrived in Jiangdong and the Song capital;
he initially translated [the scriptures] at Mount Lu and in the capital.

*Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, six fascicles; translated at Daochang Monastery on the first day of the eleventh month in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty. *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, two fascicles; currently missing. *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, forty fascicles; already included in the Vinaya catalog. *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣu-śīla-mūla*, one fascicle; currently missing. *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya*, thirteen fascicles; currently missing. *Saṃyukta-piṭaka*, one fascicle; currently missing. The Sanskrit text of the *Sūtra on the Stringing Together* (*Vyūha-sūtra*) has not yet been translated. The Sanskrit text of the *Dīrgha-āgama* has not yet been translated. The Sanskrit text of the *Saṃyukta-āgama* has not yet been translated. The Sanskrit text of the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* has not yet been translated. The Sanskrit text of the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* has not yet been translated. *Record of the Buddha’s Travels in India*, one fascicle. These eleven works [are as follows].
It was definitively compiled into six sections,
totaling sixty-three fascicles,
during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty.
The śramaṇa Shi Faxian traveled to the Western Regions in the third year of the Long’an era.
In Central India and the Kingdom of Siṃhala, he obtained the Indic original texts.
He returned to the capital and resided at Daochang Temple,
where he collaborated with the Indian Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra to jointly translate the *Dīrgha Āgama* and the *Madhyama Āgama*.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* abridgments are still in Sanskrit and have not yet been translated.
The Fangdeng Dantetu Dharani Sutra in four fascicles, also known as the Dafangdeng Dharani; this one work consists of four fascicles.
It was [translated] during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty.
Translated by the śramaṇa Shi Fazhong of Gaochang Commandery.
One fascicle of the *Pumenpin jing* (Sutra of the Universal Gate Chapter). This missing section consists of one fascicle in total.
Produced by the Śramaṇa Jīvaka from the Western Regions.
Tradition states that it appeared during the Jin dynasty.
The period of its imperial reign is unknown.
*Nirṇaya-vinaya-sūtra* (決定毘尼經), one fascicle; also known as *Destroying All Consciousness* (破壞一切心識). This single work comprises one fascicle in total.
Various catalogs all state that it was produced at Dunhuang in Liangzhou; however,
the name of the person who translated the scripture remains unknown.
The tradition states that it appeared during the Jin dynasty,
though it is not known during the reign of which emperor.

The *New Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, two fascicles, translated at Daochang Temple during the second year of the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty; one catalog states it was produced at Liheshan Temple. The *Buddhacarita*, five fascicles—also titled *Praise by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa* or *Praise of the Buddha’s Original Deeds*—produced at Liheshan Temple. These two works are listed above.
It consists of seven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty,
there was the śramaṇa Shi Baoyun.
Translated at Liohe Mountain Monastery.
*The Sutra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle. This work consists of one fascicle in total.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty,
the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema from the kingdom of Huanglong traveled through the Western Regions and translated [this work].

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* in thirty-four fascicles was translated by Shi Faxian from a Hu (foreign) manuscript he had obtained; it was rendered into Chinese in the seventh month of the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty and has already been entered into the Vinaya catalog. The *Mahīśāsaka-bhikṣu-śīla-mūla* in one fascicle appeared simultaneously with the Vinaya, and the *Mahīśāsaka-karman* in one fascicle also appeared simultaneously with the Vinaya. These constitute three works in total.
It consists of thirty-six fascicles.
During the reign of King Yingyang of the Song dynasty,
the śramaṇas Zhu Daosheng and Shi Huiyan [compiled it].
He invited the Kasmirian Vinaya Master Buddhayaśas to the Longguang Temple in the capital to translate [the work].
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* in thirteen fascicles is now missing; this constitutes one section.
It consists of thirteen fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
the Śramaṇa from the Western Regions, I-tipo-lo (Īśvarapāla), [translated it].
In the third year of the Yuanjia era,
it was translated at Pengcheng for Wang Zhongde, the Regional Inspector of Northern Xuzhou.

Before the *Vibhaṅga* (Section on Analysis) was completed, in the eighth year [of the reign], he again requested the Tripiṭaka Master to collate and edit them at the capital. These comprised four works:

the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* in ten fascicles (also known as the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* in ten fascicles); the *Upāsaka-śīla-saṃkṣepa-śāstra* in one fascicle (also titled *The Characteristics of the Five Precepts for Upāsakas: The Three Refuges and the Twenty-two Precepts for Upāsakas*); the *Dharmaguptaka-karman* in one fascicle (also known as the *Miscellaneous Karma*); and the aforementioned four sections.
It consists of thirteen fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman from Kaśmīra [translated it].

Translated at the capital (Kaiyuan). The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* in fourteen fascicles was produced at Changgan Monastery during the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty; the translation by Baoyun was completed in the ninth month of that year. The *Mātṛkā-sūtra* in ten fascicles was translated at Moling Pingle Monastery during the first month of the Binghai year, the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty; it was completed on the twenty-second day of the ninth month. The *Karmavibhaṅga-saṃkṣepa* in one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Mahāvīra; the *Rājapraśāstikā-gāthā* in one fascicle, composed by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna; and the *Āryasaṃghasnānādhivāsana-vākya* in one fascicle. These five works above are missing.
It consists of twenty-seven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman from India [translated it].

Translated in the capital (Kaiyuan): *The Scripture on the Method of Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Scripture on the Contemplation of Samantabhadra*. A sub-note states it was extracted from the *Scripture of Profound Merit*. *The Scripture on the Contemplation of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *The Scripture on the Contemplation of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva*. *The Secret Essentials of Dhyāna*, three fascicles; translated in the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era. Alternatively titled *The Essentials of the Dhyāna Method*, or five fascicles. *The Essential Methods for the Five Gates of Dhyāna*, one fascicle. The above consists of four works.
It consists of six fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
the Kasmiri meditation master Dharmamitra [translated it].
These were translated at Zhihuan Monastery during the Yuanjia period:

the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of Universal Radiance) in six fascicles; the *Sutra of the Four Heavenly Kings* in one fascicle; and the *Guangbo yanjing jing* (Sutra of Vast, Pure, and Adorned [Buddha-fields]) in four fascicles—also known as the *Guangyanjing buidu lunzhuan jing* (Sutra of the Vast Adornment and Non-retrogression Wheel)—these three works.
Eleven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
the śramaṇa Shi Zhīyán [translated this].
In the fourth year of the Yuanjia era,
it was translated together with the śramaṇa Baoyun.
The *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra* in twenty fascicles and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in one volume— these two works were missing from the Hu (foreign) originals and had not yet been translated.
It was compiled as a single collection consisting of twenty fascicles during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty.
The śramaṇa Shi Zhimeng returned from traveling in the Western Regions;
during the Yuanjia era, he translated the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* in one fascicle at Xiliangzhou.
In the fourteenth year [of that era], he brought it back to the capital.
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, thirteen fascicles, translated during the twenty-second year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty;
this single work consists of thirteen fascicles in total,
produced during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song.
The śramaṇa Shi Tánxué of Liángzhōu possessed great majestic power;
he obtained the Hu-language manuscript of this sūtra in the kingdom of Yutian and translated it at Tiān'ān Temple in Gāochāng Commandery. It was transmitted by the śramaṇa Shì Hóngshǒu.
The *New Ekottarika-āgama* in fifty fascicles; the *Mahābherī-hāraka-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated at Dong’an Temple;

the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* in one fascicle, translated at Danyang Commandery; the *Aṣṭāṅga-sukha-vihāra-sūtra* in one fascicle, translated on the thirteenth day of the first month in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era at Jingzhou; and the *Laṅkāvatāra-ratna-sūtra* in four fascicles.
*The Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, four fascicles, translated at Daochang Temple. *The Sūtra on Past and Present Causes and Effects*, four fascicles, translated at Daochang Temple.
*The Sūtra on the Continuous Liberation*, two fascicles, translated at Dong’an Temple.

*The Brief Exposition of the Five Aspects of the Ultimate Truth*, one fascicle, translated at Dong’an Temple. *The Explanation of the Sixty-two Views*, one fascicle, translated at Dong’an Temple; [text missing].
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, one fascicle; this appears to be the same as the missing one-fascicle *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, one fascicle, missing.
The *Aśoka-rāja Sūtra*, one fascicle, missing. The above consists of thirteen sections.
In seventy-three fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
the Indian Mahāyāna Dharma Master Guṇabhadra [translated this].
During the Yuanjia era and the time of Emperor Xiaowu,
various sutras were promulgated and translated by the śramaṇa Shi Baoyun and his disciple Bodhidharmavīrya.

*The Scripture on Contemplating Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Birth in Tuṣita Heaven*, one fascicle—also called *The Scripture on Contemplating Maitreya Bodhisattva* or *The Scripture on Contemplating Maitreya*. *The Scripture on the Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle. *The Secret Scripture for Healing Illnesses through the Essentials of Dhyāna*, two fascicles. Translated at Zhuyuan Temple in the second year of the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty. *The Scripture on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha-Mother*, one fascicle. Translated at Dinglin Shangsi on Mount Zhong in the second year of the Xiaojian era; also known as *The Scripture on the Parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī*. These four works above.
It consists of five fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty,
there was Juqu Anyanghou, a younger cousin of the King of Hexi of the illegitimate [Later Liang] state.
Translated in the capital (Kaijing).
The first two contemplations were previously translated long ago in Gaochang Commandery and brought to the capital.

The *Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection) in six fascicles was translated during the sixth year of the Daming era of the Song dynasty; some call it the *Pusa Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Bodhisattva’s Sutra on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection). The *Pomoduoluoni Jing* (Sutra of the Demon-Destroying Dhāraṇī), also known as the *Wuliangmen Pomoduoluoni Jing* (Sutra of the Demon-Destroying Dhāraṇī of the Immeasurable Gates), in one fascicle, was also translated in the sixth year of the Daming era. These two works constitute the right-hand section.
It consists of seven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty,
the Western Region śramaṇa Guṇabhadra arrived in Jingzhou.
The śramaṇa Shi Xuan requested that it be translated in a meditation hall.
One fascicle: *Daśabhāṇavāra-karmavācanā*, also known as the *Brief Essential Karmavācanā Method*. Translated from the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. The above constitutes one work.
One fascicle in total.
During the Jingzhong era of the Song dynasty,
the Vinaya Master Shi Sengqu [composed this].
Compiled in the capital (Kyoto).

One fascicle of the *Śāriputra-vinaya Bhikṣuṇī-Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (also known as the *Śāriputra-vinaya Bhikṣuṇī-mahāśīla*), and one fascicle of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya Karma-vastu*. The above consists of two works.
It consists of two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty,
there was the Vinaya Master Shi Faying.

Compiled in the capital of Kyoto: the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in seven fascicles (missing); the *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-sūtra* in five fascicles (missing); the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* in five fascicles (missing); the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* in ten fascicles (missing); and the *Guhyamati-tyāya-sūtra* in one fascicle, titled in the Han language *Xianren yonglü* (The Sages’ Application of Discipline), which is missing. These constitute the five aforementioned sections.
It consists of twenty-eight fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty,
there was the Indian śramaṇa Zhu Fajian.
Translated at Guangzhou, none of these reached the capital.

The *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* in thirteen fascicles is missing; the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Dharmatrāta-dharmagupta-kathā*) in six fascicles is missing; and the *Upāya-hṛdaya-śāstra* in two fascicles is missing—these three works are absent.
It consists of twenty-one fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty,
the Tripitaka Master from the Western Regions, Ji Jiaye, [translated it].
In the second year of the spurious Yanxing era, in the northern kingdom,
it was translated together with the Monastic Head (Sengzheng) Shi Tanyao;
Liu Xiaobiao received the oral dictation.
These three sutras have not yet reached the capital.
*The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings*, one fascicle. This one work consists of one fascicle in total.
During the reign of Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty, the Indian śramaṇa Dharmagatayaśas translated the *Pañcajātaka-sūtra* (The Sutra of Five Birth Stories);

its number of fascicles is unknown and it is incomplete. [Also] the *Tāpali-śīla* (The Vinaya of the Venerable Elder); its number of fascicles is unknown and it is incomplete. These two works above are missing.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty,
the foreign śramaṇa Mahāyāna translated it at Guangzhou.

Before reaching the capital, the *Śariputrabhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*) in eighteen fascicles was produced during the seventh year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty; this constitutes one work.
It consists of eighteen fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty,
there was the śramaṇa Shi Sengyi.

At Zhulin Monastery in Guangzhou, the foreign Dharma Master Saṃghabhadra was invited to translate the *Guānshìyīn Chànhuǐ Chúzuì Zhòujīng* (Sūtra of the Avalokiteśvara Repentance and Mantra for Eradicating Transgressions), one fascicle, translated on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month of the eighth year of the Yongming era; and the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Ti-pó-duō-duō Pin* (The Devadatta Chapter of the Lotus Sutra), the twelfth chapter, one fascicle. These two works comprise the above total.
It consists of two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty,
our former master presented [this work] and subsequently traveled to the Western Regions.
In the Kingdom of Khotan, he obtained a Hu-language manuscript of the Avalokiteśvara Repentance Dhāraṇī;
upon returning to the capital, he requested the Tripiṭaka Master Fayi of the Chan Hall at Waguan Temple to translate it together with him.
To the west of the shifting sands,
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* includes the "Devadatta Chapter," whereas the version transmitted in China lacks this one chapter.
My late master traveled to Gaochang Commandery,
where he obtained the original text and subsequently transcribed it to bring back to the capital.
Now, this is separately compiled as one fascicle.

The *Baiju poyu jing* (Sūtra of One Hundred Verses of Parables) consists of ten fascicles; it was translated on the tenth day of the ninth month in the tenth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, or alternatively, it comprises five fascicles. The above constitutes one work.
It consists of ten fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty,
the Indian śramaṇa Guṇavidi translated it at the capital.
*Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, one fascicle. This work consists of one fascicle in total.
It was [translated] during the reign of the Emperor of the Qi dynasty.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Fadu.
*The Dharma for Teaching and Instructing Bhikṣuṇīs*, one fascicle. This work consists of one fascicle in total.
In the third year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty,
the śramaṇa Shi Sengsheng of Lingyao Temple on Mount Zhong compiled [this work] based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The *Daizhilun chao* (Excerpts from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) in twenty fascicles, also known as the *Yaolun* (Essential Treatise).
This single work consists of twenty fascicles in total.
[Compiled] during the reign of the Jin Emperor.
The śramaṇa Shi Huiyuan of Mount Lu,
because the treatise was voluminous and difficult for students to comprehend,
has therefore abridged and excerpted its essential points.
The *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* in eight fascicles: this single work consists of eight fascicles.
It was [translated] during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty.
The śramaṇa Śengjian translated [texts] during the Qi period in the kingdom of Henan.

He produced one fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* in the second year of the Jianwu era, and one fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Elder Sudatta* in the second year of the Jianwu era; in total, he produced four hundred and fifty works.
In total, there are one thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven fascicles. 2.

New Catalogue of Scriptures of Different Translations. Regarding the "Scriptures of Different Translations" in the second volume of the New Catalogue of Scriptures of Different Translations: these are scriptures that have appeared in different versions.
This means that while the Indic originals were identical, the Chinese translations differ;
furthermore, as the Sanskrit manuscripts remained concealed, the various translators produced many variations.
The literary styles and intellectual inclinations of those who brought forth the sutras each differed.
Language may be either plain or ornate, and its meaning may be either detailed or concise;
thus, while the root is one, the branches become two, and the new and old diverge.
This occurs when the national language undergoes corruption and change.
Thus, while sounds and characters differ between the Chu and Xia regions,
if the translated phrasing and style are obstructed, the underlying facts and meanings will become as distant as Hu and Yue;
how could this be the case for the magnificent steeds transmitted from the West?
This was merely a result of errors in the transcription toward the east.
Consequently, the *Nirvāṇa* and *Laṅkāvatāra* were produced with great difficulty,
reaching as far as the seven *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
In another version, there are eight [chapters].
This occurs frequently throughout various other scriptures.
I shall now list the titles and name the individuals concerned to demonstrate their similarities and differences.
As for those various miscellaneous sūtras of uncertain origin whose translators' names are lost, they are all appended to the records of works of unknown source.

Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras: Zhi Chen translated the *Banzhou sanmei jing* (Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra) in ten fascicles; Zhu Foshuo translated the *Yiri shuo banruo jing* (Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom Spoken by the Sun) in one fascicle; the *Daoxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in one fascicle—this *Daoxing* is an excerpt from the *Prajñā*—was translated by Zhu Shixing; the *Fangguang jing* (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in twenty fascicles, also known as the *Old Xiaopin*, was translated by Zhu Fahu; the *Xiaopin jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in seven fascicles was translated again by Dharmarakṣa; Weishi Du compiled the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Daoxing jing* in two fascicles; Tanmopi translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in five fascicles, also known as the *Chang'an-pin jing*; and Kumārajīva translated the *New Dapin* (Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in twenty-four fascicles and the *Xiaopin* in seven fascicles. Thus, these last two sūtras were produced in different versions by seven individuals.

The *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* (one fascicle), translated by Zhi Chen; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (two fascicles), translated by Zhi Qian; the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* (two fascicles), translated by Dharmarakṣa; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (thirty-six fascicles), translated by Dharmakṣema; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* (six fascicles) and the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* (two fascicles), translated by Shi Faxian; and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (twenty fascicles), translated by Shi Zhimeng; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (one fascicle), translated by Guṇabhadra—these constitute one group of scriptures.
The seven individuals emerged separately.
Among them, Zhi Qian’s *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* is largely identical to the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa*.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* translated by Dharmakṣema is largely identical to that of Faxian;
the remaining three versions are all missing.
The differences between these versions are not yet clearly understood.

Among the old catalogs of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there is mention of a *Sarvapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, said to be a different recension of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; it is not yet known who produced this version, as it is currently missing. Dharmarakṣa translated the ten-fascicle *Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), and Kumārajīva translated the seven-fascicle *Xinmiaofalianhua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra). These constitute one [set of] scriptures.
Three persons departed.
One of them was lost in the translations, his name unknown;
he has already been entered into the *Shiyuan lu* (Record of Lost Sources).

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles translated by Zhi Chen; the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles translated by Zhi Qian; the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles translated by Bo Yan; the *Dhīra-vikrāmiṇa-samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles re-translated by Dharmarakṣa, which is a re-translation of the *Śūraṅgama*; the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles translated by Zhu Ji Lan; and the *New Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles newly translated by Kumārajīva. There was also a version titled the *Shu Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles listed in the old catalogs, whose translator is unknown. These constitute one sūtra.
Seven persons emerged [as translators].
One of them has lost his name due to the loss of the translation record and has already been entered into the *Shiyuan lu* (Record of Lost Sources).

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* translated by Zhi Qian in two fascicles; the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa in two fascicles, with another version in one fascicle titled *Xuan Vimalakīrti*; the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* translated by Zhu Shulan in two fascicles; and the *New Vimalakīrti-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva in three fascicles. The above constitutes one single scripture.

Four different translations were produced: the *Wuliangshou jing* (Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra) translated by Zhi Qian in two fascicles; the *Amiduojing* (Amitābha-sūtra) translated by Zhu Fahu in two fascicles, also known as the *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue*; the *Wuliangshou jing* translated by Kumārajīva in one fascicle; and the *Xin wuliangshou jing* (New Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra) translated by Shi Baoyun in two fascicles. The *Wuliangshou jing* translated by Guṇabhadra in one fascicle is listed as the final one.
Five persons translated it separately.

The *Dàodì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Path) in two fascicles was translated by An Shigao; the *Xiūxíng dàodì jīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of the Stages of the Path) in seven fascicles was translated by Zhu Fahu. The above is one sūtra.
These two were translated separately by different individuals.

The *Puyao jing* (Sūtra of Universal Radiance) in eight fascicles was translated by Zhu Fahu; the *Puyao jing* in six fascicles was translated by Shi Zhiyan. Thus, these two versions of the same sūtra were produced by two different people.

The *Bhadra-kalpika-sūtra*: translated by Dharmarakṣa in ten fascicles; translated by Kumārajīva in seven fascicles. These two versions of the same sūtra were produced separately by these two individuals.
The *Sāgara-nāgarāja-sūtra*: translated by Dharmarakṣa in four fascicles; translated by Dharmakṣema in four fascicles. These two versions of the same sūtra [are as above].
Two different translations were produced.
The *Madhyamāgama* in fifty-nine fascicles was translated by Dharmanandi; the *Madhyamāgama* in sixty fascicles was translated by Saṃghadeva. The above is one scripture.
Two different translations were produced by two individuals.

The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) was translated by Zhu Fahu in five fascicles, while Shi Faju produced a version in six fascicles; these two versions of the same scripture were produced by two different people.

The *Weimi chi jing* (Sūtra on the Subtle and Secret Retention), translated by Zhi Qian, one fascicle; and the *Weimi chi jing*, translated by Buddhabhadra, one fascicle. These two versions of the same sūtra were produced by two different individuals.

The *Da fangdeng rulai zang jing shi* (Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra) translated by Faju in one fascicle; the *Da fangdeng rulai zang jing* (Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra) translated by Buddhabhadra in one fascicle. The above is one sūtra.
Two different translations were produced by two individuals.

One scroll of the *Benye jing* (Sūtra on Original Acts) was translated by Zhi Qian; one scroll of the *Benye jing* was translated by Buddhabhadra. Thus, for this single sūtra, there are two different translations by two individuals.

The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (Ten Stages Sutra) in four fascicles translated by Kumārajīva; and the *Bodhisattvadaśabhūmika* (Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva) in one fascicle translated by Buddhabhadra. These two versions of the same sutra were produced by two different translators.

The *Sūtra of the Sun’s Transcendent Radiance* (*Chāorìmíng jīng*): two fascicles translated by Zhu Fahu; two fascicles translated by Nie Chengyuan, which are a revised and edited version of those produced by Master Fahu. Thus, there is one sūtra in total.
These two were translated by different individuals.
The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* was translated in two fascicles by Zhi Chen; the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* was also translated in two fascicles by Zhu Fahu. The above constitutes one sūtra.
Two different translations of this work exist.

One version of the *Mile chengfo jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood) was translated by Zhu Fahu; another version of the *Mile chengfo jing*, consisting of one fascicle, was translated by Kumārajīva. The above constitutes one sūtra.
These two were translated by different individuals:

the *Guanshiyin shoujue jing* was translated by Zhu Fahu; the *Guangshiyin dasheshi shoujue jing*, one fascicle, was translated by Dharmakṣema; and the *Guanshiyin shouji jing*, one fascicle—these three scriptures [are as follows].
Two different translations exist.
One fascicle of the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* was translated by Zhi Qian; one fascicle of the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* was translated by Dharmarakṣa. The above constitutes one sūtra.
These two were translated by different individuals.
One fascicle of the *Pumen jing* was translated by Zhu Fahu; one fascicle of the *Pumen pin* was translated by Jītamitra. The above constitutes one scripture.
These two were translated by different persons.
The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* was translated by Zhu Fahu in one fascicle; the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra* was translated by Guṇabhadra in four fascicles. The above constitutes one scripture.
These two were translated by different individuals.
The *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* was first translated by Zhi Chen in two fascicles; later, Zhu Fahu retranslated the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* in one fascicle. The above constitutes one scripture.
Two different translations by two individuals:

one fascicle of the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (Twelve Links of Dependent Origination) translated by An Shigao; one fascicle of the *Śālistamba-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa. The above constitutes one scripture.
These two were translated by different persons:

the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* in two fascicles was translated by Zhi Qian, while the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* in four fascicles was translated by Dharmarakṣa; these constitute one single scripture.
Two individuals translated these separately.

Kumārajīva translated the *Dhyāna Sūtra* in four fascicles and the *Essential Explanation of Dhyāna Methods* in two fascicles; Buddhabhadra translated the *Dhyāna Sūtra* in two fascicles; Dharmamitra translated the *Essentials of Dhyāna Methods* in two fascicles; and Juqu An’anghou translated the *Secret Method for Treating Illnesses through Dhyāna Essentials* in one fascicle. The above constitutes one scripture.
Four translations were produced.

*The Sūtra of Ākāśagarbha* (5 fascicles), translated by Dharmakṣema; *The King of Vaipulya: Ākāśagarbha* (1 fascicle), translated by Dharmamitra; *Ākāśagarbha* (5 fascicles), translated by Śrīghana; *Ākāśagarbha* (1 fascicle), translated by Buddhayaśas. The above constitutes one sūtra.

The *Sūtra of the Four Men’s Departure*, translated by An Shigao; one fascicle of the *Parable of the Five Aggregates*, translated by An Shigao; twenty-five fascicles of the *Sūtra of Three Hundred Parables*, translated by Zhu Fahu (without a separate title, its name remains undetermined); six fascicles of the *Dharmapada-avadāna*, translated by Shi Fa Ju; ten fascicles of the *Śatagāthā-avadāna*, translated by Guṇavīra; and ten fascicles of the *Avadāna-sūtra*, translated by Kang Fasui—these constitute the aforementioned scriptures.
Five translations were produced:

*The Sutra of Akṣayamati* in four fascicles translated by Zhu Fahu; *The Sutra of Akṣayamati* in ten fascicles translated by Zhu Fajian; and *The Akṣayamati Chapter of the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* in four fascicles translated by Dharmakṣema. Thus, these three individuals produced one sutra [in three versions].
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-saṃgraha-sūtra* (translated by Dharmakṣema), eight fascicles; the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (translated by Guṇavarman), ten fascicles. The above is one scripture.

Two persons produced [this work]. The *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* translated by Dharmatrata, one fascicle; the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* translated by Kumārajīva, one fascicle; the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the Dharmaguptaka school translated by Buddhayaśas, one fascicle; the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the Mahāsāṃghika school translated by Faxian, one fascicle; and the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the Mahīśāsaka school translated by Buddhabhadra, one fascicle. The above constitutes one scripture.
The five men came forth.
When the assembly was counted and recorded, they all said:
The two hundred and fifty precepts have appeared in six different versions.
One of these lacks a translated title and is recorded in the *Shiyuan lu* (Record of Lost Sources).

The *Bhikṣuṇī-śīla* (One Scroll), translated by Zhu Fahu; currently missing. The *Bhikṣuṇī-mahā-śīla* (One Scroll), translated by Shi Sengzhu. The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-bhikṣuṇī-śīla-mūla* (One Scroll), compiled by Shi Faying. The *Mahābhikṣuṇī-śīla* (One Scroll) transmitted by Mi Li. These are considered doubtful scriptures and are currently missing. Thus, one scripture was produced by four people.

The *Abhidharma-pañcadharma* and *Abhidharma-saptadharma*, two fascicles, translated by An Shigao; the *Saptadharma* is currently missing. The *Abhidharma-aṣṭānavatidharma*, one fascicle, is also missing.
Saṃghadeva translated the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* in fourteen fascicles and the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya* in sixteen fascicles.
Saṃghavarman translated the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* in fourteen fascicles.
The *Abhidharmahṛdaya* in four fascicles;
the *Vibhāṣā* produced in India, the *Śāriputrābhidharma* in twenty-two fascicles;
and the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā* produced by Buddhavarman in sixty fascicles.
Shi Faxian produced the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* in thirteen fascicles;
Yiye Poluo produced the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* in thirteen fascicles;
and Saṃghavarman produced the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* in fourteen fascicles.
The *Kātyāyanābhidharmahṛdaya* in twenty fascicles; it is unknown who produced this, and it has already been entered into the *Shiyuan lu*.
The above scripture was produced by nine persons in total.
The *Chengjuguangming jing* (Sūtra of the Perfectly Manifested Radiance) by Zhi Chen and Zhi Yao; the above is one scripture.
The two men produced them separately.
The *Fajing jing* was translated by An Xuan and Zhi Qian;
these are two separate translations by two different individuals.
The *Dharmapada-sūtra* translated by Zhi Nan and Zhi Qian (one scroll);
these two versions were produced by different individuals. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva and Guṇabhadra (one scroll).
Two people translated it separately.
The *Dīrgha Āgama* was translated by Buddhayaśas; the *Śāriputra Abhidharma* was translated by Faxian.
These two scriptures were produced by two different individuals.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* (translated by Faxian) and the *Śāstra on Wisdom* (translated by Zhimeng)—

these two scriptures were produced by different individuals. The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (translated by Dharmarakṣa) and the [Prajñāpāramitā] translated by Kumārajīva— these two scriptures [are as follows].
The two were translated by different individuals.
According to Master Dao’an’s *Zalu* (Miscellaneous Records), there is also this sūtra translated by Guṇavīta; thus, one of these two sūtras was produced by two different persons.
The *Vaipulya-nirvāṇa-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* translated by Faxian;
these two versions were produced separately by the two individuals.
[Recorded] in the second fascicle of the first volume of the *Chu sanzang jiji*.
Volume Three: From the *Chusanzangjiji* (Collection of Records Concerning the Translation of the Tripitaka), Middle Volume, Part Three.
Compiled by Shi Sengyou.
*Xinji Angong Guyijing Lu* (Newly Compiled Catalogue of Ancient and Extraordinary Scriptures by Master Dao’an), Number One.

New Compilation of the Catalogue of Scriptures Translated by Master Dao’an, Part Two; New Compilation of the Catalogue of Diverse Scriptures from Liangzhou by Master Dao’an, Part Three; New Compilation of the Catalogue of Diverse Scriptures from Guanzhong by Master Dao’an, Part Four; New Compilation of the Record of the Division of the Vinaya into Five Sections, Part Five; New Compilation of the Record of the Division of the Vinaya into Eighteen Sections, Part Six; New Compilation of the Record of the Four Sections of Vinaya that Reached Han Territory, Part Seven. 1. New Compilation of Master Dao’an’s Catalogue of Ancient and Diverse Scriptures. New Compilation of Master Dao’an’s Catalogue of Ancient and Diverse Scriptures, Part One. Regarding "ancient and diverse scriptures": [text continues]
This is indeed a remnant of the texts previously produced.
Examining An’s records,
they extend from the *Dàodì yāoyǔ* (Essential Words on the Stages of the Path) down to the *Sìxìng zhǎngzhě* (The Elder of the Four Castes).
In total, there are ninety-two sūtras,
which are designated as "ancient and distinct.
Although the texts have been scattered and lost, with many portions missing, they remain extant.
Examining the extant texts, one can distinguish between those of ancient and modern origin.
Some lack distinct titles and instead adopt phrases from the scriptures themselves as their headings.

Alternatively, one might abridge the four sections, selecting a single matter to establish as the title of the fascicle; this would be a substantial and authentic approach that accords with the ancient classics.
Master Dao’an, having observed its antiquity and uniqueness, appended it to the end [of his collection].
Huiyou inferred that its date was ancient and placed it at the head [of his catalog].
Although it has lost its original source, this old translation is still extant.

The *Dàodì jīng zhōng yāoyǔ zhāng* (Essential Passages from the *Dàodì jīng*), one fascicle—also known as the *Xiǎo dàodì jīng* (Shorter *Dàodì jīng*)—is now available. From [this point on], there are these scriptures.

From this point onward, those not designated as "having [a specific title]" are all missing their original numerical counts. *Lianyi zhang* (Chapter on Refining the Mind), one fascicle; the old catalog states it is the *Shu lian jing* (Sūtra on Counting and Refining).

Master Dao’an stated that the two aforementioned sūtras are derived from the *Shengsheng jing* (Sūtra of Birth). Sengyou examined the current *Sheng jing* (Sūtra of Birth) and found that this chapter name does not exist therein.

*Fan zhi Po boluoyan wen zun zhong jing* (The Sūtra of the Brahmin Pāpaya’s Questioning the Honored Lineage), one fascicle; the old catalog states it is the *Poboyan wen zhong* (Pāpaya’s Questioning of the Lineage).
The Venerable Scripture now contains the following: the *Bodhisattva-mārga-bhūmi Sūtra* in one fascicle; Master An states it is from the Vaipulya section;

Regarding the *Saṃyukta Āgama* translated by Xuánzàng, this *Saṃyukta Āgama* contains only twenty-five sūtras, yet the commentary treats them as forty-five.
Could this be due to errors caused by the scattering of characters during transcription, leading to redundant copying?

Even the ancient worthies suffered from such issues—as seen in the "three pigs" (*sānshǐ*) error recorded in the Jin annals and the "five gates" (*wǔmén) correction in the Lu chronicles—how much more so for a hired scribe? Thus it was with the Buddha’s [teachings].

2. Newly Compiled Catalogue of Scriptures of Lost Translations by Master An. This second volume of the Newly Compiled Catalogue of Scriptures of Lost Translations by Master An was collated by Sengyou.
As for those scriptures that possess translated titles, they are recorded here following the previous volume.
Those whose translators' names are unknown are listed below. Following Seng'an’s catalogue,
these range from the *Xiuxing benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Acts of Practice) down to the *He da jing* (Sutra of Heda).
In total, there are one hundred and thirty-four sūtras;
their translators are not clearly identified.
Furthermore, both the catalogs from Guanzhong and Liangzhou omit the names of the translators.
Now, these have been collectively categorized and entered into the section titled "Sources of Error.
While Master An’s catalog is indeed excellent,
I regret that it is somewhat too concise.
The titles of the sutras are noted by extracting only two characters from each;
furthermore, the fascicle numbers are not listed, and the texts are joined directly one after another.
Consequently, in later transcriptions, the names and categories became confused and intermingled.
Furthermore, red dots are used as markers;
if the red is obliterated, there is confusion.
To pursue [the truth] by following emptiness leads to being entangled in what is difficult to comprehend.
This, too, is a flaw in the *yu-fan* jade.
Furthermore, the various records and miscellaneous scriptures were collected in a haphazard manner, with many titles being redundant or duplicated, resulting in a disordered and confused arrangement.
Now, I have thoroughly revised and organized them, establishing the divisions of the volumes so that names and contents correspond, ensuring there shall be no confusion in consultation.

When the Great Way unfolds its brilliance, the ten thousand phenomena manifest their forms. It is because the essence of the Dharma is profound and subtle that its manifestations are diverse; it is because the principle of the Way is vast and expansive that its applications are manifold. Thus, from the time the Buddha appeared in the world until his entry into Nirvana, the various schools arose in succession, each establishing its own teachings. From the era of the Three Kingdoms and the Two Jin down to the present dynasty, the various masters have appeared one after another, each leaving behind their own records. Preface to the Catalogue of the Hongming ji (Collection for Elucidating and Clarifying), Number Eight, compiled by the Śramaṇa Sengyou. Now, the ocean of awakening is boundless, and the realm of wisdom shines forth in perfect clarity.
Within the wondrous realm of transformation,
he truly molds and refines the legacy of Yao and Shun;
in principle, he excels beyond the boundaries of conventional systems.
Thus, he modeled his teachings after those of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius.

He was the crown prince of the King of Parthia.
From childhood, he harbored a pure and filial piety, serving his parents with utmost sincerity.
His benevolence, rooted in compassion, extended even to the most humble creatures;
his speech and conduct were as precise as if measured by compass and square.
Furthermore, he was exceptionally intelligent and diligent, applying himself with focused resolve to his studies.
There were no foreign classics that he did not master.
He was thoroughly versed in the phenomena of the seven luminaries and the five elements,
as well as the divinations of wind-angles and atmospheric portents.
He calculated the waxing and waning of the calendar with complete mastery of its variations;
moreover, he was profoundly versed in medical arts and exceptionally skilled in acupuncture and moxibustion.
By observing a patient's complexion, he could diagnose their ailment, and his administration of medicine invariably brought about recovery.
Even birds and beasts would cry out upon hearing his voice, and from their sounds, people could discern his state of mind.
Thus, his reputation for extraordinary talent spread throughout the Western Regions;
neighboring countries, both far and near, all revered and esteemed him.
Although Lokakṣema lived as a householder,

Biography of Dharma Master Daosheng. Biography of Dharma Master Daosheng, the fourth [section].
Zhu Daosheng was a native of Pengcheng.

Starting from the senior-most monk and proceeding down to the lowest rank,
he would travel through them all before vanishing;
he did this once every year.
Xian also personally saw this dragon.
Later, when he arrived at Pāṭaliputra in Magadha within Central India, he obtained the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya at the Deva-rāja Monastery south of the Aśoka Stūpa.
Furthermore, he obtained the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-uddāna*,
the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-sūtra*,
and various sūtras such as the *Vaipulya* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
He remained for three years,
studying the Hu script and Hu language,
and personally transcribed [the texts] by hand.

Thereupon, he entrusted the sutras and images to a merchant caravan and arrived in the Kingdom of Siṃhala (Sri Lanka), where he found that more than ten of his companions had either remained behind or perished;
looking at his own reflection, he was left all alone.
Constantly harboring a sense of sorrow and lamentation,
he suddenly saw a merchant before the image of the King making an offering of a single white round fan from the land of Jin.
Unconsciously overcome with emotion, he shed tears and stayed for two years.
Furthermore, he obtained the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya, the Dīrgha-āgama, the Saṃyukta-āgama, and the Kṣudraka-piṭaka—all of which were previously unavailable in the land of Han.
Shortly thereafter, he boarded a large merchant vessel and returned to the East.
There were approximately two hundred people on board.
Encountering a violent storm, the ship was wrecked and water flooded in.
The crowd was terrified and immediately took up various items and discarded them.
Xian feared that the merchants would likewise discard his scriptures and images.
With single-minded devotion, he contemplated Avalokiteśvara and took refuge in the Sangha of the land of Han;
for thirteen days and nights, a great wind blew.
The ship was blown to the foot of an island, where they finished repairing it; however, before they had even departed,
it became dark with rain and gloom, and they did not know where they were going,
being left to drift entirely at the mercy of the wind.
If they encountered hidden rocks or bandits, not one in ten thousand would survive.
After traveling for ninety days,
they reached the country of Yavadvīpa.
He stayed for five months.
Then he again joined other merchants and headed for Guangzhou;
they raised their sails for over a month.
In the middle of the night, they were suddenly struck by a great wind;
the entire ship trembled with fear,
and the multitude deliberated together, saying:
"This śramaṇa is sitting upon us and causing us to be thrown into such distress.
We cannot allow the entire community to perish for the sake of a single individual."
He intended to cast him out.
Dharma-xian’s lay patron rebuked the merchants in a stern voice, saying,
"If you drive this śramaṇa away..."
"You should also release me;
otherwise, you shall be put to death.
The emperors of the land of Han revere the Buddha and honor the Sangha."
"I shall go there and inform the king;
he will surely punish you.
The merchants looked at one another, their faces turning pale with fear, and they reluctantly desisted.
With both water and provisions exhausted,
he could do nothing but drift with the wind and current;
suddenly reaching a shore, he saw common weeds and plants and knew at once that he was in the land of Han.
Not yet knowing in which direction to go,
he immediately boarded a small boat and entered a creek.
Searching for a village, he encountered two hunters.
Khyen asked,
"What place is this?
The hunter replied:
This was on the southern shore of Mount Lao in Changguang Commandery, Qingzhou.
A hunter returned and reported it to the Regional Governor Li Yi,
who had long been devoted to and faithful in his religious practice.
Suddenly hearing that the śramaṇa had arrived from afar,
he personally went out to welcome and greet him;
Daoxian then took the scriptures and images and returned with him.
Shortly thereafter, he wished to return south.
At that time, the Regional Inspector requested that he remain for a longer period. Hsien said:
This poor monk has cast himself into a place from which there is no returning;
his ambition was to propagate and spread [the Dharma], yet what he hoped for remains unfulfilled.
He could not remain there for long.
He then traveled south to the capital to join the foreign meditation master Buddhabhadra.

At Daochang Monastery, he translated the six-fascicle *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*, and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*; as for those works that had not yet been translated...
It comprised approximately one million words.
Once Xian had translated the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra and disseminated it for the purpose of teaching and transforming others,
everyone was enabled to see and hear it.
There was a family whose names have been lost,
residing near Zhuanju Gate. For generations,
they had upheld the orthodox teachings.
He personally transcribed one copy for recitation and offering;
as he had no separate scripture room,
it was kept in the same building as miscellaneous books.
Later, wind and fire suddenly broke out and spread to his house.
All his possessions were completely consumed,
yet only the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* remained perfectly intact.
The charred remains were not damaged, and the color of the scroll remained unchanged;
this was widely circulated throughout the capital,
where all praised it as divine and miraculous.
Later, he went to Jingzhou and passed away at Xinsi.
He was eighty-two years of age.
The assembly all mourned him with deep sorrow.

The customs he heard of and witnessed have separate biographical records. **Biography of Dharma Master Zhìyán, Number Seven.** Dharma Master Zhìyán was a monk from the land of Shu (Sichuan). It is unknown where his ancestors were from. His secular surname was Zhào. He was a man of profound character and great intelligence. From his youth, he possessed a sharp and penetrating mind; he was naturally inclined toward the Way and deeply devoted to the study of the scriptures. At first, he studied under the Venerable Huìyuǎn of Mount Lu. Later, he traveled to the capital to seek out the teachings of the various masters. He was particularly skilled at reciting the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. During the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, he translated the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in ten fascicles. Subsequently, he traveled to the Western Regions, where he obtained the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in forty fascicles. Upon returning to the capital, he translated it together with the Indian Tripiṭaka master Saṃghadeva. He also produced translations of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, and others. He died in the year of the Wuchen cycle during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, at the age of seventy-nine. His remains were interred at Mount Lu. His disciples erected a stupa for him on the mountain. His writings include the *Commentary on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in five fascicles, the *Commentary on the Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* in three fascicles, and the *Commentary on the Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* in two fascicles. These works remain extant. Furthermore, he composed the *Record of the Western Regions* in one fascicle. This concludes the biography of Dharma Master Zhìyán. 7. Having left home at the age of twenty,
he became renowned for his diligent application.
Wearing patched robes, sitting in meditation, and subsisting on vegetarian food, he remained in perpetual seclusion.
Desiring to seek widely for the sutras and the Dharma,
he traveled extensively throughout the Western Regions until he reached Jibin, where he met the meditation master Buddhabhadra.
Dharmakṣema desired to transmit the Dharma to China and,
with utmost sincerity, made a formal request.
Guṇabhadra, admiring his earnest devotion, granted his wish.
They then traveled together toward the east.
Thereupon, they crossed the Snow Mountains, enduring the bitter cold and perilous terrain, drinking ice and eating wood, frequently facing life-threatening dangers.
After traveling for several years, they finally reached Guanzhong.
Dharmabhadra had always resided at the Great Monastery in Chang’an.
Recently, however, Dharmabhadra was unjustly expelled by the monks of the Qin state.
Consequently, Huiguan and the assembly who had come from the West both dispersed and departed beyond the Passes.
He continued to reside at the Shandong Monastery,
where he sat in meditation, recited the sutras, and applied himself with diligence to his studies.
In the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he...
When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty campaigned westward against Chang’an,
he returned in triumph with his banners passing through Shandong.
At that time, Wang Huai, the Duke of Shixing, was accompanying the imperial entourage.
While traveling to visit mountains and rivers, he arrived at the Yan Monastery.
There he saw two fellow monks, each sitting on a rope-cot, their meditation so profound and serene that even after Huai had been there for a long time, he did not realize it.
Thereupon, with a snap of his fingers, the three men opened their eyes;
yet before long they closed them again and did not exchange a word with him.
Hui was moved by deep respect for his extraordinary nature.
He inquired of the local elders,
all of whom said that these three monks had lived in seclusion for many years and had never once left the mountain.
Hui immediately petitioned Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, requesting that he be invited back to the capital;
however, no one was willing to go.
After repeated requests, he finally arrived.
The two men escorted Huiyan along the way;
Huikai and Daohuai served him with such profound sincerity and meticulous ritual that their devotion was complete.
Upon returning to the capital, he immediately took up residence at Shixing Temple.
Yanxing was by nature serene and tranquil, his mind seeking to avoid the clamor and dust of the world.
Huai therefore built another vihāra on the outskirts of the eastern suburbs;
this was the Jiyuan Monastery.
Previously, while in the Western Regions, Faxian had obtained the Indic manuscripts of various sutras;

however, before he could translate and copy them, he arrived in the Song dynasty in the fourth year of the Yuanjia era (427 CE), where he, together with the śramaṇa Baoyun, translated three sections of scriptures: the *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara-sūtra), the *Guangbo yanjing* (Brahmaviśeṣacintīparipṛcchā-sūtra), and the *Sifawang jing* (Caturmahārājika-sūtra).
While residing at the monastery, he did not accept special invitations;
both monastics and laypeople from near and far respected and were moved by him.
This was even before he had left the household life.
He constantly observed the five precepts;
whenever he committed a transgression or violation,
he later entered the Way and received full ordination.
I have long harbored doubts that I did not receive the precepts,
and I have lived in constant fear of this for many years;
though I have practiced meditative contemplation, I have been unable to resolve it for myself.
He then once again crossed the sea and returned to India to consult with those of great wisdom and erudition.
There he encountered an Arhat bhikṣu,
to whom he related the matter in its entirety and questioned him.
The Arhat did not dare to reach a definitive judgment;
he therefore entered meditative absorption for Yan,
traveled to the Tuṣita Heaven, and consulted Maitreya.
Maitreya replied that he had received the precepts.
Daoyan was overjoyed;
they then returned on foot and arrived at Jibin.
He passed away without illness at the age of seventy-eight.
According to the customs of foreign lands:
Monks who had attained the Way were buried separately from ordinary monks; however,
although Huiyan’s ascetic practices were peerless,
the assembly at that time had not yet determined whether he had truly attained the Way or not.
When they attempted to bury the grave of an ordinary monk,
he raised his solemn funeral bier and refused to let it be moved;
even as more people were added to the effort, it remained motionless as before.
The multitude were all struck with wonder and astonishment.
They tried changing their direction toward the tomb of Deyi Dao,
whereupon the four men carried him along as swiftly as the wind.
Thus, he was finally able to be interred.
Later, Yan’s disciples Zhiyu and Zhida returned from the Western Regions at great distance to report this news.
They both returned to their foreign lands.
Biography of Dharma Master Baoyun, Number Eight. Regarding the biography of Dharma Master Baoyun:
his clan name is unknown.
According to family tradition,
he was a native of Liangzhou.
Having entered the monastic order in his youth, he was diligent and possessed both learning and virtuous conduct.
His character and temperament were firm and pure, making him an anomaly in his time;
thus, in his youth, he was renowned for his uprightness, integrity, and simple sincerity.
In his quest for the Dharma, he was earnest and compassionate, forgetting his own person as he pursued the Way.
Vowing to personally behold sacred traces and extensively seek out the various scriptures,
he eventually traveled far to the Western Regions at the beginning of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty.
Accompanying Faxian and Zhiyan from beginning to end,
he traversed the shifting sands and ascended the snowy peaks;
though the hardships and perils were great, he did not consider them difficult.
He then traveled through the various kingdoms of Khotan and India, witnessing many miraculous phenomena in their entirety.
Subsequently, he passed through the wilderness of the Rākṣasas and heard the sound of celestial drums.
He paid homage at many sites associated with the traces of Śākyamuni.
While abroad in foreign lands, he studied Hūṇa scripts extensively;
he was thoroughly proficient in the phonology, characters, and glossaries of all the various kingdoms of India.

Later, he returned to Chang’an, where he followed the meditation master Buddhabhadra to receive instruction and cultivate the Way. He applied himself diligently to both meditative practice and the chanting of sutras without ever flagging.
Shortly thereafter, the meditation master was unjustly expelled by the monks of the Qin court.
The entire assembly shared in his guilt,
and the clouds likewise dispersed.
Later, at Mount Lu, the monk Shi Huiyuan resolved the matter of his expulsion.
Together they returned to the capital and settled at Daochang Temple.
Because Yunzhi’s resolve was firm and fierce as he propagated the Way in distant lands, the monastic community all opened their hearts to consult him;
they held him in both reverence and affection.
Yun translated the newly produced *New Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*.
Among the various sūtras produced later,
many were translated by Yun.
He constantly held the Hu manuscript in his hand while orally interpreting it into the Jin language;
he was proficient in both Chinese and foreign tongues, and his phonology and glosses were perfectly accurate.
All those present were convinced by and accepted the standards established by Fanyun.
At the beginning of the period of the Fu and Yao dynasties,
there was the śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Chuanzhou, who was highly skilled in oral exposition and translation.
He manifested various sutras;
among those practicing Sanskrit in the region south of the Yangtze River, none surpassed Yún.
Thus, during the transition between the Jin and Song dynasties, he widely propagated the Dharma-treasury.
The śramaṇas Huìguān and others all befriended him and held him in high esteem.
Because Sēnyún by nature preferred secluded dwellings to preserve his leisure and tranquility,

I translated the *Buddhacarita-kāvya*.
The mountains there are mostly desolate and the local customs favor petty theft;

Of the ten temples that received ritual services and offerings, eight were his.

Biography of Dharma Master Zhimeng. Biography of Dharma Master Zhimeng, Number Nine. Shi Zhimeng.
He was a native of Xinfeng County, Jingzhao Commandery, Yongzhou.
By nature upright and intelligent, he cultivated his conduct with purity and integrity.
From his youth, he donned the dharma robes and devoted himself single-mindedly to his religious studies.
The sound of his chanting continued from night into day.
Whenever he saw foreign monks speak of the traces left by Śākyamuni,
or heard that the Vaipulya sūtras were spread throughout the Western Regions, [he was moved].
I have often been moved by deep emotion, directing my thoughts toward distant realms beyond.
I held the view that ten thousand *li* are but a few inches away and a millennium can be reached.
Thus, in the sixth year of the Hongshi era of the pseudo-Qin dynasty, the year Wuchen (488 CE), I set out.
He summoned fifteen fellow śramaṇas to form a group and set out from Chang’an;
they crossed rivers and followed valleys, traversing thirty-six fords.
Upon reaching the city of Liangzhou,
he subsequently traveled west out through Yangguan Pass into the shifting sands.
For more than two thousand li, the land was devoid of water and grass.
Travelers are few and far between.
In winter it is bitterly cold, while in summer it is malarial and scorching.
When people die, their bones are piled up to mark the path.
Carrying provisions on camels was an extremely arduous and perilous undertaking;
he thus traveled through the various kingdoms of Shanshan, Kucha, and Khotan,
observing their customs and manners in detail.
Traveling southwest from Khotan for two thousand li,

at that point, nine of his companions turned back.
Ming continued his journey for more than one thousand seven hundred li until he reached the country of Boliun.
There, the snow-capped cliffs of the Three-Sectioned Snow Mountains rose brilliantly to a height of over a hundred thousand *tan*.
He fashioned a bridge from flying ropes and crossed through the air.
Peering down, its bottom could not be seen; looking up, the sky was not visible.
The cold air was bitterly cruel, causing one's shadow to tremble and the soul to shudder with fear.
It was a place that neither Zhang Qian nor Gan Ying of the Han dynasty ever reached.
Traveling south again for one thousand *li*, he reached the kingdom of Jibin.
He crossed the Indus River a second time;
the clouds and mountains rose up like sheer cliffs, even more formidable than before.
Below, obstructing vapors and malevolent spirits abound, cutting off the path;
many practitioners die there.
Only those with fierce sincerity and penetrating insight can traverse the perils and reach safety.
Having arrived at the city of Kaśmīra,
five hundred arhats constantly reside within this kingdom and frequently travel back and forth to Lake Anavatapta.
There was a venerable Arhat who,
seeing that Meng had arrived and come to rest, rejoiced and praised him.
Meng inquired about the local lands, and [the Arhat] spoke to him of the affairs of the four heavenly kings.
These details are all contained in his biography.
Previously, Xuangmeng had seen a stone spittoon inscribed with the Buddha’s writing in the country of Kiśa;

however, when he lowered the case, he again perceived no weight.

The towering ice increases in height until it is utterly devoid of grass or trees;

On the flanks of the eastern and western mountains,
ropes were fastened to form bridges;
they were five li apart from one another.
Ten people pass by one after another;
having reached the other shore,
they raise smoke as a signal.
When those behind see smoke, they know that the person ahead has already crossed;
only then can they proceed further.
If they do not see smoke for a long time, they know that a violent wind has blown the rope away and the person has fallen into the river.
After traveling across the Pamir Mountains for three days, he finally passed over them.
He then ascended the Snow Mountains,
where precipitous cliffs rose sheer like walls, leaving no place to set foot.
The stone walls were all provided with old wooden peg holes facing one another at regular intervals.
Each person took hold of four pegs;
first pulling out the lower peg, they then grasped the upper peg with their hands.
They took turns replacing one another for three days before finally passing away;
they then reached level ground where they waited for one another to conduct an inventory,
during which twelve of their companions were lost.
He proceeded to the kingdom of Kaśmīra,
where he paid homage to the Buddha’s almsbowl and stayed for over a year.
Having completed his studies of the Hu (Kharoṣṭhī) script, he subsequently mastered the Hu language.
He obtained one fascicle of the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* in Sanskrit.
Accompanied by thirteen other śramaṇas traveling together with him,
he traveled westward to reach Sindhu-nadī.
In the language of Han, it is called the Lion-Mouth River.
To the west, it enters the kingdom of Yuezhi,
where one may pay homage to the Buddha’s *uṣṇīṣa* bone.
He also saw his own wooden boat boiling over.
Later, he arrived at the Shiliu Monastery on the southern side of Mount Dantaka,
where three hundred monks were practicing the various teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Wujie then stayed at this monastery to receive full ordination.
The Indian śramaṇa Buddhataila— whose name means "Buddha-Rescuer" (Fojiu) in the Qi language— [was present].
The assembly of monks from that region said,
"Since he has attained the fruits of the Path,
Wujie requests him to serve as his preceptor."
The Chinese śramaṇa Zhiding served as an ācārya for three months during the summer retreat at the monastery;
thereafter, he traveled northward to Central India.
In these desolate regions, he always carried rock honey as his provisions.
Of his eight companions, eight died along the way;
only five proceeded together.
Having repeatedly encountered perilous and thorny situations,
he never exhausted the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* he carried with him,
constantly focusing his mind and maintaining mindfulness of it.
As he proceeded through the kingdom of Śrāvastī,
he encountered a herd of wild elephants in the wilderness.
Sudhana called out their names and took refuge in them.
Immediately, a lion emerged from the forest;
the elephant, struck with terror, fled,
and later crossed the Ganges.
Furthermore, he encountered a herd of wild oxen coming toward him with bellowing roars,
intending to harm him;
Wujie took refuge [in the Buddha] as he had done before.
Soon after, a large vulture flew over, causing the wild oxen to scatter in alarm;
he was thus able to escape.
That his sincere heart moved such a response, enabling him to overcome danger and achieve deliverance, is entirely of this nature.
Later, he traveled by ship across the South Sea from Southern India and arrived at Guangzhou;
his various experiences along the way are recorded in a separate biography.
Among the works he translated was the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
Now it is transmitted in the capital; his final whereabouts are unknown.
Excerpted from the *Chū-sanzō-ki-shū*, Volume 15, Part 2 of the Biographies.
